copy.llms.summary: Women Can Code: women who build real software with AI, and understand it well enough to own it. In 10 days you ship a working tool for your own life, job or business, with AI as your pair programmer and the founder live alongside you. The days follow GitHub Skills exercises (credited to GitHub, linked, never rehosted) in your own GitHub account. Day 1 is open to everyone; the full 10 days, with live calls, open with the first wave, and you can register interest now. Everyone who finishes gets a free product to keep: their tool hosted on Ontold, their own domain set up, and a listing on the womenintech.me outputs leaderboard, on terms the founder confirms.

about.lead: Women Can Code is for women who build real software with AI, and understand it well enough to own it. The skill is not memorising syntax. It is describing what you want, reading what the AI made, spotting when it is wrong and fixing it, putting it live, and keeping it safe.
about.description: What {name} is for: building your own software with AI, and understanding it well enough to own it.

sections.html: Five things, on a real project of your own: describing what you want, reading what the AI made, spotting when it is wrong and fixing it, putting it live, and keeping it safe (data, keys, privacy and costs). See the 10 days.

sections.q: How is this different from WomenWithAI?
sections.html: WomenWithAI is about using AI in everyday life and work. {name} is about building your own software with AI.

The days follow free GitHub Skills exercises, made and run by GitHub, in your own GitHub account. We link to them and never copy them, and GitHub does not endorse us. Other free courses (The Odin Project, freeCodeCamp, MDN, CS50, Python for Everybody) are on the go deeper shelf.
Anyone who identifies as a woman and has something she wants to build: for her own life, her job or her business. No experience needed.
If a course changes, moves or stops being free, tell us and we will fix or remove it.

guidelines.description: The rules moderators apply to every WomenABC submission: true, positive, kind, properly credited, and about women.

sections.html: Name the people, say when it happened, and give a source or an official page if there is one. If a moderator cannot confirm it, it waits. Personal achievements that are not public record (a graduation, a first exhibition, a small business opening) are welcome when the person themselves or someone close to them submits them.
An award, a record, a release, a launch, a rescue, a repair, a reunion. The test: would the people in it be glad to see it here?
No entry is built on someone else's failure, and nothing here mocks, shames or exposes anyone. That includes rivals, other countries, men, and other women.
Submit links to the official page, the publisher, the label, the gallery or the article, not to copies. We do not host files; we point to where the work lives.
People who identify as women, anywhere; we take a person's own description and do not question it. Groups and teams count when women are at the heart of them.

sections.h: 6. No advertising, no politics for its own sake
sections.html: A product launch by a woman founder is a story. An advert is not. A woman elected to office is a story; campaigning is not. Open doors into public life list the way in (a placement, a public appointment, how to stand as a councillor) and never a party or a position; a scheme run by one party is listed only beside the equivalent from every other. Moderators use judgement and err towards kindness.

Your email is never shown and is used only to ask you a question about your submission. Your name is shown as "shared by" only if you give it. We store a one-way hash of your network address for one hour to slow down floods, not the address itself.
Anyone named in an entry can ask for it to be corrected or removed, and it will be. Send a correction.

coders.lead: Ada Lovelace is often considered the first computer programmer. Women have been coding ever since: programming languages, compilers, the Apollo flight software, the networks behind the internet.

people.name: Ada Lovelace
people.built: Worked on Charles Babbage's analytical engine, and is often considered the first computer programmer.

people.name: Grace Hopper
people.built: Developed the FLOW-MATIC programming language, a major influence on COBOL, and was one of the first programmers on the Harvard Mark I.

people.name: Dorothy Vaughan
people.built: Taught herself and her staff the Fortran programming language at NASA Langley.

people.name: Katherine Johnson
people.built: Her orbital mechanics calculations were critical to the first US crewed spaceflights.

people.name: Mary Jackson
people.built: Started as a computer at NACA, and in 1958 became NASA's first black female engineer.

credit.by: NASA Langley Research Center, Bob Nye

people.name: Annie Easley
people.built: A computer scientist who contributed to the beginning iterations of NASA's rocket technologies.

people.name: Frances Allen
people.built: A pioneer of optimizing compilers, and in 2006 the first woman to win the Turing Award.

people.name: Margaret Hamilton
people.built: Led the development of the on-board flight software for NASA's Apollo Guidance Computer.

people.name: Barbara Liskov
people.built: Introduced abstract data types and the Liskov substitution principle; 2008 Turing Award.

people.name: Radia Perlman
people.built: Invented the Spanning Tree Protocol, fundamental to how network bridges work.

days.title: Your first live page
days.build: A web page you described to the AI, live at an address you can share within about 30 minutes, and you have read every line of it.
days.about: Follows GitHub Skills, GitHub Pages: you copy the exercise into your own GitHub account and GitHub Actions checks each step. GitHub says the exercise takes less than one hour. You need a free GitHub account and a browser.
steps: Sign in to your free GitHub account and open the GitHub Skills GitHub Pages exercise.
Copy the exercise to your account, as its page shows, and wait for the first step to appear.
Describe the page you want to an AI assistant in plain words, and ask it for the HTML.
Put the page in your repository, then read every line and ask the AI about any line you cannot explain.
Turn on GitHub Pages as the exercise shows, and open your live address.

faq.a: Most days follow a free GitHub Skills exercise, made and run by GitHub. You do it in your own copy of the exercise in your own GitHub account. We link to it and never copy it, and GitHub does not endorse us. Where no GitHub Skills exercise fits, the day says so and links a free course from MDN or The Odin Project.

faq.q: Can I take one level on its own?
faq.a: Yes. Level 1, Build it, is for beginners and ends with your tool live on GitHub Pages. Level 2, Make it real, takes a tool further and ends on your own domain at demo day. Each level has its own Register interest and its own certificate.

faq.q: Do I need to pay for anything?
faq.a: You need a free GitHub account. AI subscriptions such as Claude, ChatGPT or Cursor are optional, and you never need to set up API billing. Try it: Day 1 is open now. The 10 days come in two 5-day levels that open with the first wave, and you can register interest in each level now.
No. Day 1 starts with describing a page in plain words.

faq.q: What do I get at the end?
faq.a: Finish Level 1 and you get your Level 1 certificate; finish Level 2 and you get your Level 2 certificate. Each is its own verifiable certificate, issued by the founder. Everyone who finishes Level 2 also gets their launched tool hosted free on Ontold, their own domain set up for them, and a listing on the womenintech.me outputs leaderboard. The exact terms are set out on this page and are to be confirmed.
Wave 1 dates are to be announced. Day 1 is open now.
